opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, when Shubho first said he was seriously considering it, my first reaction was almost disbelief. He had built a really strong track record at Meta, working on large-scale AI infrastructure and research, and he could have gone almost anywhere. And here I was, a very young founder with a big, somewhat crazy idea about building AI that can reason in mathematics, at the level of a research mathematician.

What convinced me it could work was the conversations we had. They weren't really recruiting conversations; they felt more like two people getting excited about the same problem. I come from the math side. I care a lot about formal proofs, about Lean, about what it means for a machine to actually *understand* a mathematical argument rather than just pattern-match. Shubho comes from the systems and scaling side. He knows what it takes to train models at serious scale, how to build the infrastructure, and where things break. I realized very quickly that the thing we wanted to build needed both halves, and that I couldn't fake the second half.

There was also a trust question. When you bring in someone that senior as a very early member, you have to ask yourself, "Will this person respect the vision, and will I be secure enough to let them push back on me?" With Shubho, I felt both. He challenged me a lot, on timelines, on what's actually feasible, but always in a way that made the plan better rather than smaller.

So I'd say I thought of it as a bet, on both sides. He was betting on a mission and on me. I was betting that combining deep math with world-class engineering was the right recipe. Looking back, I think it was one of the most important decisions for the company. It also sent a signal to other people we wanted to hire: if someone like Shubho believes in this, maybe it's not so crazy after all.

r001.rationale: The response describes betting on the mission and combining math with engineering, but does not say Carina wanted the company to succeed or perform well enough to be worthy of its joiners.

fable-5.1.text:
When Shubho joined, honestly, I thought of it as the single most important thing that had happened to the company up to that point.

I was coming at this from the math side. I had spent years in the world of competition math and then research math, and I had a very clear conviction about what the problem was: that mathematics is the one domain where you can actually verify the truth of what a model produces, and that if you build a system around formal verification, you get a flywheel that doesn't exist anywhere else in AI. But conviction about the problem isn't the same thing as knowing how to build the infrastructure to attack it at scale.

Shubho had spent a long time doing exactly that kind of work, large-scale systems, training infrastructure, the unglamorous engineering that decides whether a research idea becomes a real system or stays a paper. He had seen several generations of this field up close. So when we started talking, what struck me was not that he was impressed by the vision. A lot of people were impressed by the vision. It was that he immediately started asking the hard questions about data, about compute efficiency, about how the verification loop would actually run in practice, and those were the questions I knew I needed a partner to answer.

I also thought about it in terms of risk. For someone at his stage, with his options, to leave a very comfortable position and join a company that at the time was essentially a thesis and a handful of people, that was a real bet. And it told me something about how he evaluated the opportunity, because he is not a romantic about these things. He is a very grounded engineer. If he thought it was worth it, that gave me a lot of confidence that the thesis was not just something I believed because I happened to love math.

And then the last piece, which I think people underrate, is temperament. Early companies are stressful, and the founding relationship matters as much as the technology. Shubho is steady. When something breaks, he does not panic, he goes and fixes it. I am more of the person who sets the direction and pushes hard, and having someone next to me who is calm and deeply technical and willing to say "no, that won't work, here is why" has made the company better. So at the time I thought of it as a huge win, and looking back I would say I underestimated how much of a win it was.

r001.rationale: The response describes Shubho’s technical contributions, risk-taking, and temperament, but does not say Carina wanted the company’s work to be worthy of the people joining it.

Especially early on, someone joining can really shape the company. So it’s not just about how talented someone is—it’s about the kind of team you can build together.
